[Ultralytics](https://www.ultralytics.com) creates cutting-edge, state-of-the-art (SOTA) [YOLO models](https://www.ultralytics.com/yolo) built on years of foundational research in computer vision and AI. Constantly updated for performance and flexibility, our models are **fast**, **accurate**, and **easy to use**. They excel at [object detection](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/detect), [instance segmentation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/segment), [semantic segmentation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/semantic), [depth estimation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/depth), [image classification](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/classify), [pose estimation](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/pose), and [oriented object detection](https://docs.ultralytics.com/tasks/obb) tasks, and can [track](https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track) detected objects across video frames. Usage ### CLI You can use Ultralytics YOLO directly from the Command Line Interface (CLI) with the `yolo` command: ```bash # Predict using a pretrained YOLO model (e.g., YOLO26n) on an image yolo predict model=yolo26n.pt source='https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg' ``` The `yolo` command supports various tasks and modes, accepting additional arguments like `imgsz=640`. Explore the YOLO [CLI Docs](https://docs.ultralytics.com/usage/cli) for more examples. ### Python Ultralytics YOLO can also be integrated directly into your Python projects. It accepts the same [configuration arguments](https://docs.ultralytics.com/usage/cfg) as the CLI: ```python from ultralytics import YOLO # Load a pretrained YOLO26n model model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") # Train the model on the COCO8 dataset for 100 epochs train_results = model.train( data="coco8.yaml", # Path to dataset configuration file epochs=100, # Number of training epochs imgsz=640, # Image size for training device="cpu", # Device to run on (e.g., 'cpu', 0, [0,1,2,3]) ) # Evaluate the model's performance on the validation set metrics = model.val() # Perform object detection on an image results = model("path/to/image.jpg") # Predict on an image results[0].show() # Display results # Export the model to ONNX format for deployment path = model.export(format="onnx") # Returns the path to the exported model ``` Discover more examples in the YOLO [Python Docs](https://docs.ultralytics.com/usage/python).

[Tracking](https://docs.ultralytics.com/modes/track) mode is compatible with Detection, Segmentation, Pose, and OBB models. Ultralytics creates cutting-edge, state-of-the-art (SOTA) YOLO models built on years of foundational research in computer vision and AI. Constantly updated for performance and flexibility, our models are fast, accurate, and easy to use. They excel at object detection, instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, image classification, pose estimation, and oriented object detection tasks, and can track detected objects across video frames.

Find detailed documentation in the Ultralytics Docs. Get support via GitHub Issues. Join discussions on Discord, Reddit, and the Ultralytics Community Forums!

Request an Enterprise License for commercial use at Ultralytics Licensing.

📄 Documentation

See below for quickstart installation and usage examples. For comprehensive guidance on training, validation, prediction, and deployment, refer to our full Ultralytics Docs.

Install

Install the ultralytics package, including all requirements, in a Python>=3.8 environment with PyTorch>=1.8.

pip install ultralytics

For alternative installation methods, including Conda, Docker, and building from source via Git, please consult the Quickstart Guide.

Usage

CLI

You can use Ultralytics YOLO directly from the Command Line Interface (CLI) with the yolo command:

# Predict using a pretrained YOLO model (e.g., YOLO26n) on an image
yolo predict model=yolo26n.pt source='https://ultralytics.com/images/bus.jpg'

The yolo command supports various tasks and modes, accepting additional arguments like imgsz=640. Explore the YOLO CLI Docs for more examples.

Python

Ultralytics YOLO can also be integrated directly into your Python projects. It accepts the same configuration arguments as the CLI:

from ultralytics import YOLO

# Load a pretrained YOLO26n model
model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")

# Train the model on the COCO8 dataset for 100 epochs
train_results = model.train(
    data="coco8.yaml",  # Path to dataset configuration file
    epochs=100,  # Number of training epochs
    imgsz=640,  # Image size for training
    device="cpu",  # Device to run on (e.g., 'cpu', 0, [0,1,2,3])
)

# Evaluate the model's performance on the validation set
metrics = model.val()

# Perform object detection on an image
results = model("path/to/image.jpg")  # Predict on an image
results[0].show()  # Display results

# Export the model to ONNX format for deployment
path = model.export(format="onnx")  # Returns the path to the exported model

Discover more examples in the YOLO Python Docs.

✨ Models

YOLO27 — Coming Soon: Preview the upcoming family, currently undergoing final R&D. Models are not yet available, and no launch date is set.

Ultralytics supports a wide range of YOLO models, from early versions like YOLOv3 to the latest YOLO26. The tables below showcase YOLO26 models pretrained on COCO for Detection, Segmentation, and Pose Estimation. Semantic Segmentation models are pretrained on Cityscapes, Depth Estimation models are pretrained on a broad multi-dataset mix and evaluated on NYU Depth V2, Classification models are pretrained on ImageNet, and OBB models are pretrained on DOTAv1. Tracking mode is compatible with Detection, Segmentation, Pose, and OBB models. The listed pretrained models download automatically from the latest Ultralytics release on first use.

releases.body:
## 🌟 Summary
**v8.4.211 speeds up compiled SAM image encoding and expands model deployment options, with additional gains and fixes across training, OCR, and exports.**

## 📊 Key Changes
- 🚀 **Faster compiled SAM 3 and SAM 3.1:** The image encoders run **7–9% faster** in the tested `torch.compile` setup. The optimization is specific to compiled execution; eager-mode results remain unchanged.
- 📦 **Static INT8 export for ExecuTorch:** Models can now be exported in a smaller INT8 format with calibration data. Detection, segmentation, pose, and oriented-box heads remain in FP32 to help preserve prediction quality.
- 📝 **Faster OCR on NVIDIA GPUs:** OCR can use a cached FP16 TensorRT engine, which the release reports is about **2.5× faster than ONNX Runtime on dense pages** after its initial engine build. The OCR guide also clarifies which writing systems the default recognizer supports.
- ⚡ **Faster deterministic training:** Semantic segmentation and depth workloads use a faster resizing path when deterministic mode is enabled; measured speedups reached **3.9×** for one semantic segmentation setup.

releases.name: v8.4.210 - ultralytics 8.4.210 Use PyTorch device names for OpenVINO and LiteRT Intel CPU, GPU and NPU (#27136)
releases.body:
## 🌟 Summary
Release `v8.4.210` makes hardware selection more consistent across model formats, improves OCR for rotated text, and fixes several deployment and inference issues.

## 📊 Key Changes
- **One device naming convention — the main change:** OpenVINO and LiteRT now accept PyTorch-style device names. Use `cpu` for Intel CPU, `xpu` for Intel GPU, and `npu` for an Intel NPU with those runtimes. The `intel:cpu`, `intel:gpu`, and `intel:npu` names still work as deprecated aliases, with a warning. Device names are consistent, but their hardware mapping depends on the runtime—for example, PyTorch `npu` refers to Ascend, while OpenVINO and LiteRT use Intel NPU.
- **More capable OCR:** The OCR solution now uses PP-OCRv6 through ONNX Runtime, with YOLO26x-Text as its default detector. It can handle pages rotated sideways or upside down, group words into lines, and return them in reading order, without requiring PaddlePaddle. The optimized recognizer requires Python 3.11+ and ONNX Runtime 1.26+.

releases.name: v8.4.209 - Correct results for every request when serving YOLO to many users at once (#27140)
releases.body:
## 🌟 Summary
**v8.4.209 makes concurrent YOLO predictions more reliable and includes targeted fixes for validation, exports, and device-specific inference.**

## 📊 Key Changes
- **Correct results for concurrent requests:** Each prediction now applies its own settings—such as confidence threshold, IoU threshold, and image size—while holding the predictor’s inference lock. This prevents one request from accidentally using another request’s settings. The shared predictor still processes calls one at a time, so this improves correctness rather than parallel throughput.
- **More accurate validation filtering:** `val(classes=[...])` now filters predictions as well as ground-truth labels, so excluded classes are less likely to affect metrics or saved results.
- **Safer NCNN exports:** NCNN does not support a batch axis. Requests to export with `batch > 1` are now rejected before conversion, rather than potentially producing a model that crashes during prediction.
- **Fixes for specific hardware and precision cases:** Updates address mask-IoU accuracy under mixed precision, ONNX Runtime thread usage, ONNX inference on Apple MPS, Core AI export on Apple silicon, and OpenVINO exports and b

releases.name: v8.4.208 - `ultralytics 8.4.208` Release the 0.5 predict NMS IoU default (#27102)
releases.body:
## 🌟 Summary
Ultralytics **8.4.208** ships practical inference, visualization, and performance updates—most notably a **0.5 default NMS IoU for prediction and tracking**, while validation keeps its 0.7 default.

## 📊 Key Changes
- 🎯 **More selective prediction and tracking:** When `iou` is not specified, prediction and tracking now use `0.5` instead of `0.7`. Validation remains at `0.7`, and explicitly provided values still take precedence.
- 🖼️ **Better YOLOE visual-prompt results:** Calls using visual prompts now default to `conf=0.05`, helping retain more similar objects whose confidence scores may be low. Other prediction calls are unchanged.
- 🎨 **Custom class colors:** Class colors can be supplied with dataset metadata and carried through trained or exported models into prediction visualizations.
- ⚡ **Performance improvements:** Multi-GPU training with gradient accumulation avoids unnecessary gradient synchronization on batches that do not update the optimizer. NMS-free TensorRT 11 FP16 exports can also be up to 3% faster.
- 🌍 **Italian documentation access:** Italian links were added to documentation, README, and example notebook language bars.

releases.name: v8.4.207 - `ultralytics 8.4.207` Fix PaddlePaddle export on new installs and CUDA machines (#27088)
releases.body:
## 🌟 Summary
**Ultralytics 8.4.207 restores reliable PaddlePaddle export and inference, while refreshing several Docker base images.**

## 📊 Key Changes
- 🐛 **Fixed PaddlePaddle setup:** Adds the missing `six` dependency required by `x2paddle`, which could break exports in fresh environments.
- 🎮 **Improved Paddle GPU handling:** A shared setup check now recognizes installed GPU builds and avoids replacing them with CPU builds. Export, inference, and PaddleOCR use this check.
- ✅ **Re-enabled Paddle export testing:** CI now tests both exporting a model to Paddle format and running inference with the exported model.
- 🐳 **Updated Docker images:** The AMD GPU image moves to Ubuntu 26.04 and Python 3.14; the NVIDIA ARM64 image updates to NVIDIA PyTorch 26.10, CUDA 13.4, and TensorRT 11.4. Other images use refreshed floating Debian tags.

aiSummary.oneLiner: The official framework for YOLOv8, offering state-of-the-art object detection and image segmentation.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: This repository contains the Ultralytics framework, the official home of the highly acclaimed YOLO (You Only Look Once) vision models, specifically YOLOv8. It provides a comprehensive suite for training, validating, and deploying state-of-the-art computer vision models. The framework simplifies complex tasks like object detection, instance segmentation, and image classification into an accessible, unified API. It is heavily optimized for inference speed and accuracy, making it suitable for real-time applications on edge devices. The project includes extensive documentation and tools for dataset management and model exporting to various formats.
keyFeatures: Unified API: Offers a single, consistent interface for detection, segmentation, and classification tasks.
High performance: Delivers cutting-edge accuracy and inference speeds suitable for real-time video analysis.
Broad export support: Easily exports models to formats like ONNX, TensorRT, and CoreML for diverse deployment.
Built-in dataset tools: Provides utilities to automatically format and validate common vision datasets.
Pre-trained models: Includes a vast library of highly accurate models pre-trained on the COCO dataset.
